One of the best turn based games and monster catchers out there. You explore the world recording Beasts with a magical cassette player hence the name Cassette Beasts and then transform into any Beast you’ve successfully recorded. It’s a clever twist on the genre that actually feels meaningful in battle rather than just cosmetic. The game fully commits to its music theme, and it really works. The soundtrack does a lot of heavy lifting for the atmosphere, with vocal tracks kicking in when you enter buildings or key moments. It’s catchy to the point where some songs will absolutely get stuck in your head, but it adds so much personality that I wouldn’t have it any other way. There’s also a surprisingly solid social sim layer. You choose which NPCs to bring along, build relationships with them, and even partner up with a dog. These companions aren’t just there for flavor they fight alongside

Honestly, I don’t usually play turn-based games. They never really grabbed my attention, and the last one I played was Pokemon… about ten years ago. Since then, I just felt like that genre wasn’t for me anymore.
But I decided to give this game a chance because the art style really caught my eye — and I have to say, this game is a hidden gem.

The art direction is incredible. The characters, the monsters, the environments — everything looks great. But what really surprised me was the music: the way the game uses the cassette concept and turns it into the heart of the culture within its universe is just brilliant.

Another thing I loved is that the game constantly gives you something new. There are always fresh abilities, tools, or challenges — even late in the game. Because of that, it never feels repetitive.

The game gives you several questlines at once, but you can travel across the map only to discover that you need another traversal ability, a higher level, or a different quest completed first. The Ranger Captains are scattered everywhere, and losing can mean a long trip back because checkpoints and fast travel are not always convenient. Wild encounters also interrupt exploration constantly, while normal battles and repeated animations become repetitive. Even some quests feel like busywork, such as collecting 300 Wood early in the game just to build a sign. The game can be fun, but too much of that fun is buried under grinding, backtracking, unclear progression, and unnecessary frustration.
